title: Tell me about a technical decision you would make differently today.
description: Learn how to answer the technical regret interview question with self-awareness and growth. Covers what to share, how to frame regret without undermining your past work, and what interviewers are really evaluating.

data.text: This question is a self-awareness test. Interviewers want to know if you can look back at your work honestly, identify where your thinking has evolved, and show that you have changed your behavior as a result. The right answer is not about beating yourself up — it is about showing that you have grown, and that you make better decisions today because of what you learned yesterday.
What Makes a Good 'Decision I Would Redo' Story

A good story has three parts: the original decision and why it seemed right at the time, the information or perspective you have now that changes the picture, and the specific change in how you make decisions today. The contrast between then and now is the signal — if everything you would do differently is obvious and trivial, the story is not very informative.

items: The original context: What information you had and why the decision made sense at the time
The new perspective: What you learned later that changes how you see the decision
The behavioral change: A specific way your decision-making process has changed
A later application: How you applied the lesson in a subsequent decision

data.text: Start by describing the decision and the context. Be honest about why it seemed like the right call at the time — do not act like the mistake was obvious in retrospect. Then explain what you would do differently and, most importantly, how that lesson showed up in a later decision. The follow-up application is what turns a regret into a growth story.

items: The decision: What you chose and the context at the time
Why it seemed right: The data, assumptions, or constraints you were working with
What changed: New information, unexpected consequences, or a shift in your perspective
What you would do differently: A specific alternative, not a vague 'I would plan better'
How you applied the lesson: A later decision where you did things differently as a result

data.text: Example: Choosing a Database That Could Not Scale

A realistic regret story is choosing a technology based on current needs without accounting for growth. The decision was reasonable at the time but became a problem as the product scaled. The lesson is about horizon planning — building for where the system will be, not just where it is.

data.title: Sample Answer Outline
data.content:
Two years ago, I chose a NoSQL document database for a product catalog service. At the time, the catalog had about fifty thousand items, the schema was changing every sprint as we added product attributes, and the team was small. A document database seemed like a great fit: flexible schema, fast reads, and easy to iterate on.

Within a year, the catalog had grown to two million items, the schema had stabilized, and we started running into performance problems with aggregation queries. The document database did not support the relational queries we now needed, and we were writing application-level joins that were slow and fragile. Migrating to a relational database took three months of engineering time that we could have avoided.

I would make the decision differently today. I would choose a relational database from the start, with a flexible schema using JSON columns for the attributes that were still changing. That approach would have given us the schema flexibility we needed early on and the query power we needed later, without a migration.

The lesson changed how I evaluate technology choices. Now I always ask: what will this system look like in two years, not just what does it look like today? I also include a migration cost estimate in every technology proposal, even when migration seems unlikely. Six months later, when we chose a caching layer for a different service, I used that framework. We chose Redis with a structured key design that would be easy to evolve, and we are still on that system eighteen months later without needing a migration.

data.text: Interviewers are assessing three things: whether you have enough experience to have made meaningful mistakes, whether you understand why those mistakes happened, and whether you have actually changed your approach. An answer that says 'I would have done more research' without a concrete later example of doing more research is weak. Interviewers want proof that the lesson stuck.

terms.definition: Evaluating technology and architecture decisions against future growth, not just current requirements
The engineering time, risk, and user impact of changing a technology decision after it is in production
The expected scale, complexity, and usage pattern of a system over its lifetime

data.title: Common Pitfall
data.text: Do not choose a decision where the mistake was obvious to everyone, or where you would make a different choice purely because technology has improved since then. Interviewers want a story where the information was genuinely ambiguous at the time, and your later perspective is what changed the picture.
Showing Growth Without Undermining Your Past Work

It is natural to worry that admitting a mistake will make you look incompetent. The opposite is usually true. Engineers who cannot identify past mistakes often have not grown much. The key is to explain the original context clearly enough that the interviewer can see why the decision made sense, then show the new information that changed your mind. This framing makes you look thoughtful, not foolish.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Explain the original context so the mistake is understandable, not just regrettable
Show the specific lesson, not a vague 'I should have planned better'
Prove the lesson stuck by describing a later decision where you applied it
Avoid trivial or hindsight-obvious mistakes — choose a decision with real ambiguity
Self-awareness and growth are the signals, not the technical details of the mistake
